umm-al-quwain/ib-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma and Middle Years Programme subjects over live video, one-to-one. Each works with a shared screen, a writing surface the student can see, and the student's own papers, so the session is a working hour rather than a conversation about the week.

intro.heading: The sixty minutes, described honestly
paragraphs: Parents in Umm Al Quwain are rarely sceptical about whether online tutoring exists. They are sceptical about whether it does anything. A teenager, a laptop and an unfamiliar adult in another time zone is a plausible description of a wasted hour, and plenty of online tutoring deserves that description. The way to settle it is not reassurance but mechanics: what is on screen, who is writing, what is printed, what is timed, what comes back.

A working session has a shape. It opens with the marked work from last time, five or ten minutes spent on the specific marks lost rather than on the grade. Then a taught segment, with the tutor writing on a shared surface the student can see, and the student writing back rather than watching. Then a short piece of work attempted live, under something close to examination conditions, so the difficulty surfaces while somebody is there to see it. It closes by setting the next task and writing the note that goes to the parent.

The mechanics matter more here than in a city. Umm Al Quwain is the least populous emirate, and most of its Diploma students attend school in Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah, arriving home in the middle of the afternoon with a short evening and a long deadline list. The hour has to be productive on the first attempt, because there is no second hour available later in the week.

Delivery is one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to any UAE address - that is an India-only service and there is no UAE centre - and the reason that suits this emirate is supply rather than convenience. A student here sitting Higher Level Chemistry may be the only candidate in their postcode doing so, and the specialist who knows that mark scheme almost certainly lives somewhere else.

The pages that sell online tutoring usually stop at the word convenient. This one keeps going into the parts that go wrong: a student who reads a paper on a screen and never sits one on paper, a graphical calculator nobody can see, lab data that cannot be collected at home, a slot that drifts because the tutor is in a different time zone, and a recording policy nobody asked about. Each has a practical answer, and each is below.

What none of it produces is a promised grade. Nobody can offer one, and a service that quotes a predicted score before it has read a piece of your child's work is selling confidence rather than assessment. What a well-run hour over video produces is narrower and more useful: a named weakness, a method practised while somebody was watching, a timed script marked against the published scheme, and a short note you can read a month later to see whether the same problem is still being named.

Papers are sat on printed sheets to time and photographed back for marking

umm-al-quwain/ib-online-tutor.programmesIntro: What online delivery changes differs by programme. The notes below set out what works well over video in each one and what has to stay inside the school.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed against four published criteria per subject, so most of the work over video is criterion literacy: reading a strand aloud, then finding the sentence in the student's own task that meets it. Shorter sessions work better at this age, and a parent within earshot for the first fortnight helps more than it hinders.
programmes.countryNote: Younger students in this emirate often come to a session straight off a long bus run, so a forty-five or sixty-minute slot with a break beats ninety minutes. Where attention is the main obstacle rather than understanding, we say so at the trial rather than selling a longer booking.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The programme online delivery suits best, because almost everything that earns marks is writeable and shareable: papers, mark schemes, criteria, diagrams, calculator work, draft documents. The only components that cannot cross the screen are the physical practicals and the school-supervised core deadlines, both of which stay where they belong.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students here are enrolled in another emirate, so the tutor works from that school's internal deadline list. The scheduling advantage of video is specific: the slot does not move when the Sharjah road does, and the student's revision week stays the shape it was planned in.

programmes.name: The core: TOK, the Extended Essay and CAS
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are supervised at school and written by the student. Over video a tutor can read criteria, question a research question until it is answerable, and comment on a draft the student has written. Creativity, Activity, Service is a school process and sits outside tutoring entirely.
programmes.countryNote: The core is the first thing to slip when a commute is long, so sessions here are often used simply to hold a student to their school's draft dates. That is a legitimate and surprisingly effective use of an hour a fortnight in the first Diploma year.

programmes.name: Mandatory UAE subjects
programmes.description: Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum under the Ministry's general regulations. These subjects are taught from the school's own scheme of work, because using different or additional content for them requires prior Ministry permission.
programmes.countryNote: Private schools in Umm Al Quwain are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, so the school is the authority on how these subjects are timetabled and reported. Any online support has to follow the school's material rather than an imported syllabus.

umm-al-quwain/ib-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: Some subjects transfer to video almost perfectly and others need a workaround. These entries say which is which, and what the workaround is.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Works well, provided both sides can write where the other can see. The tutor shares a writing surface; the student works on paper under a second camera or photographs each attempt. What must not happen is a session where the tutor writes and the student only watches, which produces understanding without fluency.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Needs the calculator on screen. Much of this course is keystroke technique on a graphical calculator, so the tutor either shares an emulator view or asks the student to share their screen or point a camera at the handset. Describing keystrokes aloud is where online maths tuition most often fails.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Theory, mechanisms and data analysis transfer cleanly, and data questions are easier over a shared screen than on paper because a graph can be annotated live. The physical practical stays at school; what a tutor adds is research design before the lab session and analysis and evaluation afterwards.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Diagram-heavy and therefore well suited to a shared surface, where a free-body diagram can be built step by step. The habit to enforce is symbols before numbers, which is visible over video only if the student is writing too. Apparatus work remains the school's.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Recall-heavy, which online handles well through spoken questioning: a student who has to answer aloud cannot hide behind a highlighted textbook. Diagrams are annotated on the shared screen, and terminology precision is corrected in the moment rather than a week later on a returned script.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Transfers almost completely. Extracts are shared on screen and annotated together, and the individual oral is rehearsed over video in conditions close to the real thing, including the timing. Essay work is marked at sentence level in a shared document, which is more legible than handwriting in a margin.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Management
subjects.description: Diagram construction is the main online skill: building a diagram live and then using it in an argument, rather than importing a finished one. Case-study practice works well because the material is text, and commentary drafts are read criterion by criterion in a shared document.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Methodology and the statistics section of the experimental report are the most useful things to do over video, because a spreadsheet can be shared and worked through line by line. Study evaluation is taught by questioning aloud, which exposes a list of limitations pretending to be a judgement.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Suited to video because it is almost entirely discussion, and the tutor's job is to ask the question the student has not asked themselves. The essay is written by the student and supervised by the school; what happens online is criteria reading and interrogation of a draft.

subjects.name: Arabic and Islamic Education
subjects.levels: First language and additional language streams
subjects.description: Taught from the school's own scheme of work, since additional or different content for these mandatory subjects requires prior Ministry permission. Online delivery is straightforward for the language work, with the proviso that the school's material and its language of instruction govern what is covered.

sections.heading: Sixty minutes, minute by minute
paragraphs: The most common failure in online tutoring is not technical. It is a conversation that feels useful and leaves nothing behind. The protection against it is a structure the student can predict, so the hour spends its minutes on the things that earn marks rather than on settling in.

The opening ten minutes belong to the previous week's marked work, specifically to the marks lost. Not the score - the losses, named. This both closes the loop on set work and tells the tutor whether the correction was understood or copied. The middle thirty minutes are taught, with both sides writing. The last twenty are an attempt made live, under something close to examination conditions, followed by setting the next task and writing the note that goes to the parent.

There are two reasons for the live attempt rather than finishing with explanation. The first is that a student who can follow a worked example often cannot start a blank question, and that gap is invisible until they try with somebody watching. The second is honesty about what has been achieved: an hour that ends with the student producing something is a different hour from one that ends with the tutor having explained something.

The parent note at the end is short and specific - what was covered, what was set, what to watch. Its purpose is not reassurance. It is so that four weeks later a family can look at four notes and see whether the same issue is being named each time, which is the question that matters at the six-week review.

sections.heading: Sitting a real paper when the tutor is not in the room
paragraphs: A screen is a comfortable place to read a paper and a bad place to sit one. Scrolling changes how a student allocates time, a keyboard removes the handwriting that will actually be marked, and nobody who has only ever worked through papers on a laptop is prepared for three hours with a pen. So the paper gets printed.

The method is deliberately low technology. The student prints the paper, sits it to time without the tutor present, photographs or scans the script and sends it in. The tutor marks it to the published scheme, showing method marks separately from answer marks and applying the error-carried-forward rule, and the next session is spent on the script rather than on the paper. The absence of the tutor during the attempt is the point: supervision changes the result.

Three details make the difference between useful evidence and a wasted afternoon. Time it properly, including the reading time the real paper allows. Use the correct paper for the course and level, including the Higher Level third paper, which students meet least often and which rewards sustained problem-solving nobody practises by accident. And photograph every page, including working crossed out, because crossed-out working is where method marks hide.

Where printing is difficult, the fallback is handwriting answers on blank paper against a paper read on a second screen. It is not as good, but it preserves the handwriting and the timing, which are the two things that matter most. What does not work is typing answers to a maths or science paper, and we will say so rather than pretend the evidence means something.

sections.heading: The graphical calculator problem, and how a screen solves it
paragraphs: A large share of marks in both IB mathematics courses, and a meaningful share in the sciences, depends on handling a graphical calculator correctly under time pressure. This is pure technique: which menu, which window settings, how to read a root or an intersection, when to use the solver and when the examiner expects working written out instead.

In a room, a tutor glances at the handset and sees the error. Over video, the same thing happens faster, because the calculator can be put on screen. The practical options are an emulator view shared by the tutor, the student sharing their own screen if using a computer-based version, or simply pointing a phone camera at the handset so both can see the keys. Any of the three beats describing keystrokes aloud, which is the single most common way online maths tuition wastes an hour.

Model matters. Students in this region commonly use a Texas Instruments or Casio graphical calculator, and the menus differ enough that advice for one is useless on the other. A tutor should ask which model the student will sit the examination with in the first session and work with that one throughout. A student who learns on a different handset from the one they will be examined on has learned the wrong thing.

Beyond keystrokes sits the judgement question: when a calculator answer needs mathematical reasoning written beside it. On the calculator papers, a correct figure with no supporting argument loses marks the student believes they have earned. That distinction is taught by marking, and it is one of the clearest returns from the screen-share format.
bullets: Put the calculator on screen rather than describing the keys
Ask which model will be used in the examination, and use only that

sections.heading: Practicals, lab data and what stays with the school
paragraphs: Here is the honest boundary. Physical practical work in Biology, Chemistry and Physics happens in the school laboratory, supervised by the school, and no online arrangement replaces it. Anybody suggesting that apparatus work can be done over video is selling something that does not exist.

What can be done over video is most of what the Internal Assessment is actually marked on. Research design is a planning conversation: a question narrow enough to answer, a variable genuinely controlled, a method somebody else could repeat. That conversation belongs before the lab session, and having it late is the most common reason a scientific investigation caps in the middle bands however good the laboratory work was.

After the practical, data analysis and evaluation are well suited to a shared screen. Uncertainties, significant figures, graph choice, whether a line of best fit is justified, whether the conclusion refers to the data - all of this is easier to teach on an annotated spreadsheet than on paper. And evaluation, which carries equal weight with design in the current criteria, is a discussion skill: a tutor asks what the limitation actually does to the conclusion until the student stops listing and starts weighing.

The division is therefore clean rather than awkward. The school supplies apparatus, supervision and the data. The tutor supplies design before, and analysis, evaluation and criterion auditing after. The student writes every assessed word, which is both an IB requirement and the only way the work is worth anything.

sections.heading: Time zones, Gulf Standard Time and a slot that holds
paragraphs: A tutor matched by subject rather than by geography may be several time zones away, and that is the one genuine complication of the online format. It is handled by arithmetic rather than by goodwill: the session time is quoted and fixed in Gulf Standard Time, and whoever has to get up early or stay up late is the tutor, not the student.

For an Umm Al Quwain family this is more valuable than it sounds. The evening window after a commute from Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah is short, and the single most damaging thing to a tutoring arrangement is a weekly renegotiation of the hour. A fixed slot survives a term; a flexible one quietly disappears into it, usually in the week something important is due.

The practical pattern across the emirate is a 4.30pm to 5pm start for students schooling in Ras Al Khaimah, and 6pm to 7.30pm for those travelling to Sharjah or Ajman. Earlier is better than later for the hardest subject, because attention after a long bus run falls away faster than most parents expect. One subject per evening works better than two, even when the second looks affordable in the diary.

Daylight saving in other countries shifts the gap twice a year, which can move a tutor's local time without moving the student's. The fix is simply to agree that Gulf Standard Time is the reference and let the tutor's end absorb the change. During Ramadan the pattern shifts again, usually to after Iftar with sixty minutes instead of ninety, and because nothing travels, that change costs nothing but a message.

sections.heading: The setup: what makes the hour work
paragraphs: Almost every complaint about online tutoring that is not about the tutor is about the setup, and the fixes are small. Ordinary household broadband across Umm Al Quwain handles one-to-one video with screen sharing; bandwidth is rarely the real problem. The real problems are a shared room, a single device and no paper.

A headset is the first thing we ask for, because it fixes two things at once: the student hears a quiet explanation clearly, and an open microphone in a family living room stops broadcasting the household. A second device is the next, so a paper or an extract can be read full size while the conversation continues on the first. A printer is the third, because a timed paper on printed sheets is the best evidence available and typing is not a substitute.

A writing surface for the student matters as much as one for the tutor. That can be a tablet and stylus, or simply paper with a phone propped to show it. What it cannot be is nothing, because a session where only the tutor writes produces a student who recognises methods they cannot execute. We check this in the trial and say so if it is missing.

One more thing, specific to families here. A door that closes is worth more than any upgrade to the equipment. Where the only available space is shared - which is common - a later slot after younger siblings are settled often produces a better hour than an earlier one in a busy room.

sections.heading: Availability: what happens when nobody covers the subject
paragraphs: No tutoring service covers every subject at every level at every hour, and most pages in this market simply decline to mention it. Stating it plainly is more useful, particularly in an emirate where a student may be the only local candidate in their course.

Common Diploma subjects at both levels are usually matched quickly. Niche combinations take longer: a less commonly taught Group 1 or Group 2 language, a specialist Group 6 subject, or a particular Higher Level option paper. Where a UAE-based tutor is not available for a given subject and level, the match may be made with a specialist based elsewhere, teaching over the same live video format and the same Gulf Standard Time slot. That should be disclosed before a family commits, not discovered afterwards.

Where nobody suitable is available at all, the honest answer is to say so and suggest an alternative - a related subject specialist who can cover the shared skills, a shorter diagnostic block rather than a weekly commitment, or simply a recommendation to approach the school first. A family told no early is better served than one placed with a tutor who has not taught the course.

Timing matters too. The weeks before a session are the busiest in the year and the slots available then are the ones nobody wants. A family thinking about support for the final year is better off arranging it in the first term, when the choice of specialist is real, than in the term the papers are sat.

sections.heading: Recording, privacy and academic honesty online
paragraphs: Three questions parents should ask any online tutor, and rarely do. Is the session recorded, and if so who holds the recording and for how long? What personal information about my child is collected and why? And what exactly will the tutor do, and refuse to do, with assessed work?

On recording, the answer should be explicit and should be the family's choice rather than a default. A recording can be genuinely useful - a student revisiting a worked method the night before a test - but it is a file containing a minor's face and voice, and it should exist only with consent and for a stated period. A service that records by default without saying so has answered a different question from the one you asked.

On data, lead forms for tutoring collect information about children, and the UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection sits behind this. What is collected should be limited to what the match requires - subject, level, school, year group - with a stated purpose, a privacy policy reachable from the page and a route to deletion. A form asking for a child's grades, school and photograph without saying why is asking for too much.

On academic honesty the line does not change because the session is on a screen, though the temptation does. A tutor explains criteria, teaches method, discusses a research question and reads a draft the student has written. A tutor does not supply paragraphs, does not rewrite a draft to completion, and does not sit beside a student during an assessment. Sharing a screen during a school assessment is not tutoring; it is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student.
bullets: Recording is opt-in, with a stated holder and retention period
Only match-relevant information about a student is collected
A privacy route to deletion should exist and be reachable

faqs.answer: The first ten minutes go on last week's marked work, specifically the marks lost rather than the score, which also shows whether the correction was understood or copied. The next fifteen are taught, with the tutor writing on a shared surface and the student writing alongside. Then fifteen minutes of guided practice led by the student, and fifteen on an attempt made unaided under near-examination conditions. The last five set the next task and produce the written note that goes to the parent. The structure exists so the hour ends with the student having produced something.

faqs.question: Can my child really sit a past paper properly over video?
faqs.answer: Yes, but not on the screen. The paper is printed, sat to time without the tutor present, then photographed or scanned and sent in for marking against the published scheme. Scrolling distorts how a student allocates time and a keyboard removes the handwriting that will be marked, so a paper worked through on a laptop is poor evidence. Time it with the reading time the real paper allows, use the correct paper for the level including the Higher Level third paper, and photograph every page including crossed-out working, because method marks hide there.

faqs.question: How does a tutor teach graphical calculator technique remotely?
faqs.answer: By putting the calculator on screen. Either the tutor shares an emulator view, or the student shares their own screen, or a phone camera is pointed at the handset so both can see the keys. All three beat describing keystrokes aloud, which is the commonest way online maths tuition wastes an hour. The model matters: menus differ between Texas Instruments and Casio handsets, so the tutor should ask in the first session which one the student will sit the examination with and use only that throughout.

faqs.question: What happens with science practicals if the tutor is not in the lab?
faqs.answer: Practical work stays at school, supervised by the school, and nobody should claim otherwise. What a tutor adds sits either side of it. Before the lab: narrowing the research question until it is answerable and checking a variable is genuinely controlled, which is where investigations most often cap in the middle bands. After the lab: uncertainties, significant figures, graph choice, whether a conclusion refers to the data, and an evaluation that weighs rather than lists. All of that works well on a shared, annotated spreadsheet, and the student writes every assessed word.

faqs.question: Our tutor is in a different time zone. Will the lesson time keep moving?
faqs.answer: It should not. The slot is quoted and fixed in Gulf Standard Time and stays there, and where daylight saving in another country shifts the gap, the tutor's end absorbs it rather than the student's. This matters more in this emirate than in Dubai because the evening after a commute from Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah is short, and a weekly renegotiation of the hour is how a tutoring arrangement quietly ends - usually in the week something important is due at school.

faqs.question: What time of day works best for a student commuting out of Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families assume, and one subject only. Students schooling in Ras Al Khaimah are often home soon after 3.45pm and do well at 4.30pm or 5pm. Those travelling to Sharjah or Ajman usually need 6pm to 7.30pm, and from Falaj Al Mualla later still. Put the hardest subject in the earliest viable slot, because attention after a long bus run falls away faster than parents expect, and resist stacking two subjects on one evening even when the diary looks willing.

faqs.question: What equipment do we actually need at home?
faqs.answer: Less than you would think, in a specific order. A headset first, because it makes a quiet explanation audible and stops an open microphone broadcasting the household. A second device next, so a paper or extract can be read full size while the conversation continues. A printer third, for timed papers. And a writing surface for the student - a tablet and stylus, or paper with a phone propped to show it. Ordinary household broadband across this emirate is sufficient; bandwidth is rarely the real obstacle, and a room with a door matters more.

faqs.question: Is the session recorded, and who keeps the recording?
faqs.answer: That should be the family's decision rather than a default, and the answer should be explicit before the first session. A recording can be useful - a student revisiting a worked method the night before a test - but it is a file containing a minor's face and voice, so it should exist only with consent, with a stated holder and a stated retention period. If a service records by default and has not told you, it has answered a different question from the one you asked, and that is worth noticing early.

faqs.question: What information do you collect about my child, and why?
faqs.answer: Only what the match requires: subject, level, year group, school and the contact details needed to arrange sessions. The UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs personal data here, and a tutoring enquiry form is collecting data about a minor. A form asking for a child's grades, school and photograph without stating a purpose is asking for too much. There should be a reachable privacy policy and a route to deletion, and you should be able to find both without asking.

faqs.question: Could a tutor help during an online school assessment?
faqs.answer: No, and the request should be refused firmly. A tutor present during an assessment, on a screen or otherwise, is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student rather than on the tutor. The line does not change because the session happens over video, although the temptation does. What a tutor legitimately does is explain assessment criteria, teach method, discuss a research question and comment on a draft the student has written themselves - which is where nearly all the available improvement actually sits.

faqs.question: Which IB subjects transfer worst to online teaching?
faqs.answer: None transfer badly if the setup is right, but two need deliberate workarounds. Mathematics fails when only the tutor writes, so both sides need a visible writing surface and the student must work during the hour rather than watch. The sciences need the physical practical to stay at school, with design before and analysis after handled online. Subjects that are mostly text and discussion - the languages, Theory of Knowledge, Economics, Psychology, Business Management - transfer almost completely, and essay marking in a shared document is more legible than handwriting in a margin.

faqs.question: What if no tutor is available for my child's subject and level?
faqs.answer: We say so. Common Diploma subjects at both levels are usually matched quickly, while niche languages and specialist Higher Level option papers take longer. Where no UAE-based specialist is free for a subject, the match may be with a tutor based elsewhere teaching over the same live video format in the same Gulf Standard Time slot, and that is disclosed before any commitment rather than discovered later. Where nobody suitable is available, the honest answer is a shorter diagnostic block or a recommendation to approach the school first.

faqs.question: How long should an online session be for a Middle Years Programme student?
faqs.answer: Shorter than for a Diploma student. Forty-five or sixty minutes with a break usually beats ninety, particularly for a child arriving home from a long bus run. The work at this stage is mostly criterion literacy: reading a strand of criterion A to D aloud and finding the sentence in the student's own task that meets it. A parent within earshot for the first fortnight helps rather than hinders, because it establishes what the hour is for before the habit sets.

faqs.question: How do we know the online hour is working, rather than just happening?
faqs.answer: Read the parent notes together after a month. Each session should produce a short note saying what was covered, what was set and what to watch, and four of them side by side answer the question directly: is the same issue being named every week? If it is, the diagnosis is probably right and the method is not changing, so the response is timed conditions instead of untimed work, or one topic rebuilt from the beginning. If the notes are vague or absent, that is the thing to raise, and it is a fair six-week conversation.

umm-al-quwain/ib-online-tutor.closingHeading: Test the format, not the brochure
umm-al-quwain/ib-online-tutor.closingBody: The way to find out whether live video sessions suit your child is to run one. Send the subject, the level and the evening window you can genuinely keep each week, and we will arrange a free trial with the tutor who would teach - a working hour, not a sales call. It will test the tutor and the setup at the same time: whether your child can be heard, whether they can write where the tutor can see, and whether the slot survives contact with a school night in Umm Al Quwain. You will get a written diagnostic either way, and nobody will offer you a predicted grade.

intro.heading: What an IB tutor is actually being hired to do
paragraphs: Parents in Umm Al Quwain searching for an IB tutor are rarely asking for general academic help. They are asking because a report came home with a 4 in a subject the student thought they understood, or because an Internal Assessment draft came back with criterion marks that made no sense, or because the Diploma suddenly stopped resembling the Middle Years Programme the child had coped with comfortably for three years.

The Diploma is a marking system before it is a curriculum, and that is the part schools have least time to explain. A student can know the content of a subject and still lose a grade because they wrote four paragraphs when the question said outline, or because they treated the Internal Assessment as an essay when the criteria were rewarding research design. Nothing about that is a capability problem. It is a mechanics problem, and mechanics is what one-to-one sessions fix fastest.

So this page is built around the marking. It sets out how the 45 points are assembled, what the Internal Assessment is worth in each subject group and what its criteria actually reward, how command terms map to the assessment objectives, and where in each group students reliably lose marks. A parent who reads it should be able to look at their child's last report and work out which of those four things is going wrong.

Umm Al Quwain adds one practical constraint that shapes everything. It is the least populous emirate, and most internationally schooled students here travel to Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah for a school offering the Diploma. That commute eats the end of the afternoon. A child who leaves at 6.30am and reaches home at 4.30pm has a narrow evening window, and any tutoring arrangement that also requires somebody to drive is competing for the same minutes.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video, and in this emirate that is less a compromise than the reason the thing works at all. The slot stays fixed because nothing travels to it, and the student is matched with a subject specialist rather than with whoever could reach Al Salamah by seven in the evening.

One further thing is worth saying before the detail starts. Nobody can promise a grade, and the Diploma is a two-year qualification in which the largest single variable is what the student does in the hours nobody is watching. What a weekly session can reliably produce is a named weakness, a method for attacking it, and marked evidence every fortnight that a parent can read without a teaching background. Judge any arrangement on those three things at the six-week mark, and treat a tutor who offers a predicted score instead as having told you something useful about themselves.

umm-al-quwain/ib-tutor.programmesIntro: Students in this emirate reach the Diploma through several routes, and each route arrives with a different gap. The notes below describe what each programme assesses and what it looks like for a family based in Umm Al Quwain.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed against four criteria per subject, A to D, each marked out of 8 and reported on a 1-7 scale through published grade boundaries. There are no external papers in most MYP subjects, so students learn to write against criteria rather than against mark schemes, and the Personal Project in the final year is the first substantial independent piece.
programmes.countryNote: For an Umm Al Quwain family the MYP years are the cheapest time to intervene. The jump into the Diploma is where the commute and the workload collide, and a student who leaves MYP without secure algebra or essay structure will spend the first Diploma year catching up on both while the new content keeps arriving.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across the subject groups, usually three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, each graded 1-7, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Up to 3 further points come from the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge matrix, giving a maximum of 45, and the Diploma requires at least 24 points with several additional conditions.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students here are usually in a school in another emirate, which means the school's internal deadlines, mock weeks and parent evenings all run on another emirate's calendar. Any tutoring plan has to be built from the school's own deadline list rather than from a generic IB year.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme and the IB core
programmes.description: Where offered, the Career-related Programme combines Diploma courses with a career-related study and its own core, including a reflective project. Across all IB programmes the core carries assessment weight and its own internal deadlines, so Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay compete directly with subject revision in the second year.
programmes.countryNote: Provision is limited in the northern emirates, so a family in Umm Al Quwain considering it should check directly with the school rather than assume availability. Where a student is on the Diploma instead, the core deadlines are usually the first thing to slip when a commute is long.

programmes.name: Mandatory UAE subjects alongside the IB
programmes.description: Private schools in the UAE must provide Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside the international curriculum they are licensed for, following the Ministry's general regulations. These subjects occupy timetable hours and carry their own reporting, which is often overlooked when a Diploma revision plan is drawn up.
programmes.countryNote: Private schools in Umm Al Quwain are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education rather than by an emirate authority, so requirements should be confirmed with the school. Arabic and Islamic education are also excluded from the five-subject count used in the British-track equivalency rule.

umm-al-quwain/ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects Umm Al Quwain families ask about most, with what each one assesses and the point at which marks start going missing. Weightings follow the current subject guides; confirm them against your child's own guide, since the IB revises subjects on a rolling cycle.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: At SL the two papers carry 40% each with the exploration at 20%; at HL there are three papers at 30%, 30% and 20% with the exploration at 20%. HL Paper 3 is the long problem-solving paper and the one students meet least often in practice. Marks go missing in unjustified algebraic steps and in proof questions abandoned halfway.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The same paper structure as Analysis and Approaches but a modelling and statistics emphasis, with heavier graphical calculator use. Students lose marks by giving a calculator answer with no mathematical reasoning attached, and by rounding mid-calculation. Choosing between AA and AI should follow the university course in mind, not the perceived difficulty.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Papers covering multiple choice, data analysis and extended response, with the scientific investigation at 20%. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms are where HL candidates separate. The most common avoidable loss is in data questions: uncertainties omitted, significant figures inconsistent, and conclusions stated without reference to the data that supports them.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A broad syllabus where the examiner rewards precision over coverage. Students who revise by rereading lose marks on process questions requiring sequence and on command terms demanding evaluation rather than description. The investigation rewards a tightly controlled research design far more than an ambitious topic.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, fields, waves, electricity and thermodynamics, with extended response questions that require working shown in symbols before numbers. The recurring failure is unit and magnitude error under time pressure, and HL candidates often lose marks by starting from a formula rather than from the physical situation described.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay, the individual oral and, at HL, an additional essay. The individual oral is where a global issue must be genuinely connected to two extracts rather than mentioned beside them. Most lost marks come from students summarising texts instead of analysing the choices the writer made.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram-driven papers plus the Internal Assessment, which is three commentaries on published news articles, each within a strict word limit. Marks are lost when a diagram is drawn without being used in the argument, and when a commentary explains the article instead of applying the theory to it.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study examination with a pre-released case for part of the assessment, plus the Internal Assessment. Students who know the tools still cap in the middle because they apply a framework without judging its usefulness in the specific context. Evaluation, not recall, is where the available marks sit.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Biological, cognitive and sociocultural approaches with research methodology running through every question. The Internal Assessment is an experimental study report with a rigid structure, and students lose marks on the inferential statistics section and on an evaluation that lists limitations without weighing them.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Arabic
subjects.description: The Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition and the 4,000-word Extended Essay both have strict limits and school-set internal deadlines, and together they carry up to 3 Diploma points. Arabic and Islamic Education run alongside, taught from the school's own scheme because additional content requires prior Ministry permission.

sections.heading: How the 45 points are built, and which ones a tutor can move
paragraphs: A Diploma candidate is marked out of 45. Six subjects contribute up to 7 points each, giving 42, and up to 3 further points come from the matrix combining the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge grades. Creativity, Activity, Service carries no points but must be completed. The Diploma itself requires at least 24 points along with several further conditions, which is why a student sitting on 25 with one failing condition is in a more precarious position than the total suggests.

Within a subject, the marks arrive from two directions. Internal Assessment is produced at school, marked by the teacher against published criteria and moderated by the IB. External components are marked by examiners who have never met the student and who are working strictly from the mark scheme. Those two halves fail in different ways, and conflating them is the most common planning error a family makes.

This matters for deciding where tutoring hours go. External marks respond to practice: timed papers, command-term work, accuracy under pressure. Internal Assessment marks respond to process: a sharper research question, a tighter design, an evaluation that weighs rather than lists. A student losing marks on both needs the hours split deliberately, usually with the Internal Assessment first because its deadline is earlier and it cannot be retaken in the way a paper can.

What a tutor cannot do is move the core points by writing any part of the Extended Essay or the Theory of Knowledge essay. Those are supervised at school for exactly that reason. A tutor can explain the assessment criteria, discuss the research question, and read a draft the student has written - and for most students that is where the third point actually comes from.

sections.heading: Internal Assessment by subject group, and what the criteria reward
paragraphs: The Internal Assessment is the single most misunderstood part of the Diploma, and the one where a parent can see the clearest return from tutoring. Every subject has one, each takes a different form, and in most subjects it carries around a fifth of the final grade. A student who treats it as homework has already lost marks that the papers will have to make up.

The sciences assess a scientific investigation marked across criteria covering research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. Mathematics assesses an exploration marked on presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics, with use of mathematics carrying the largest single allocation. Economics requires a portfolio of commentaries on published articles, each within a tight word limit. History requires a historical investigation with its own source-evaluation section, and Psychology an experimental report with a statistics section students routinely underestimate.

Read across those, a pattern appears: the criteria reward method, not ambition. A modest research question answered with a controlled design and an honest evaluation scores better than a dramatic question answered loosely. This is the single most useful thing a tutor can tell a student in the first Internal Assessment conversation, and it usually arrives too late because the topic has already been chosen.

The second pattern is that criteria are published and specific. A student can read the descriptor for the top band of each criterion and audit their own draft against it, line by line. That is a teachable skill, it is entirely legitimate, and it is what an Internal Assessment coaching block is for. Check the mark allocations against your child's own subject guide, since the IB revises them on a rolling cycle.

sections.heading: Command terms: where two marks disappear between "state" and "evaluate"
paragraphs: IB questions are built from command terms, and each term sits at one of three assessment objective levels. The lowest asks for recall: state, define, list, identify. The middle asks for understanding and application: describe, outline, explain, apply, calculate. The highest asks for judgement: analyse, evaluate, discuss, justify, compare and contrast, to what extent.

The marks follow the level, and so does the expected length. A student who writes a paragraph for a term asking them to state has spent time they will need later. A student who writes a paragraph for a term asking them to evaluate has usually described two things and judged neither, which scores in the lower band regardless of how accurate the content is. Both errors are invisible to the student, because the content in front of them is correct.

This is the most efficient thing to fix in a short tutoring block. It requires no new content, it applies across every subject the student takes, and it is diagnosable from any marked paper. The method is mechanical: take a marked script, find the command term in each question, and check whether the shape of the answer matches the term. Students who do this twice usually stop making the error.

It also explains a common and confusing report pattern - strong in class, weaker in examinations. Classroom discussion rewards knowing things, and examinations reward answering the question in the form it was asked. A student can be genuinely strong on the first and consistently penalised on the second, and no amount of further content revision will close that gap.

sections.heading: Where Diploma students lose marks, group by group
paragraphs: Lost marks are more predictable than students expect. In mathematics they concentrate in unjustified steps: an answer that is correct but arrives without the reasoning the mark scheme credits, or a graphical calculator result quoted with no mathematical argument attached. Rounding during a calculation rather than at the end costs accuracy marks in both courses, and at Higher Level the third paper punishes a student who has never practised sustained problem-solving against the clock.

In the sciences the pattern sits in data. Uncertainties are omitted, significant figures drift between lines, graphs are drawn without considering whether a line of best fit is justified, and conclusions are stated without reference to the data that supports them. These are examination-paper losses and Internal Assessment losses at the same time, which makes them unusually efficient to fix - one skill, two places it pays.

In the humanities and languages the losses are structural. Essays summarise rather than argue, paragraphs state a point without evidence or without linking it back to the question, and the final paragraph restates the introduction rather than reaching a judgement. In Economics the diagram appears but is never used; in Business Management a framework is applied but never assessed for usefulness; in Psychology limitations are listed but not weighed.

The diagnosis is the same in every case and it does not require a new textbook. It requires two or three pieces of the student's own marked work, read against the mark scheme or the criteria, with the lost marks named. That is what a first session should produce, and a parent should be able to read the result without a teaching background.

sections.heading: The commute, and what it leaves of a school night
paragraphs: Umm Al Quwain is the least populous emirate, and its Diploma students mostly study somewhere else. A family in Al Salamah or Al Raas whose child attends a school in Sharjah or Ajman is running a commute of an hour or more each way, on a bus that leaves early and arrives back in the middle of the afternoon. By the time a uniform is off and something has been eaten, the usable evening is two or three hours long, and the core deadlines are competing for it with six subjects.

This is why the format of tutoring matters more here than the brand of it. An arrangement that requires an adult to drive into the emirate for a one-hour session is spending the same scarce window on travel, and it is the first thing to collapse in a busy term. A session delivered over live video starts at the time it says it starts, which over a two-year Diploma is worth more than any single lesson.

The practical scheduling advice from families in this emirate is consistent. Put the hardest subject in the earliest viable slot rather than the latest, because attention falls away faster than most parents expect after a long commute. Keep one subject per evening rather than two. And set the slot in Gulf Standard Time and leave it alone, since the tutor may be in a different time zone and a weekly negotiation over the hour is how a slot quietly disappears.

During Ramadan the pattern changes and should be allowed to. Families commonly move sessions to after Iftar and shorten them from ninety minutes to sixty, with a lighter load in the first week. The exam calendar does not move, so the right response is to plan the shift in advance rather than lose three weeks to it.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with the core
paragraphs: The Extended Essay, the Theory of Knowledge essay and every Internal Assessment are the student's own work, and the IB treats that as an integrity requirement rather than a convention. The boundary is worth stating plainly, because at least one provider in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a fixed price, and the consequence of that transaction falls on the student.

Inside the boundary a tutor can do a great deal. They can explain what each criterion rewards and what the top descriptor actually asks for. They can discuss a research question until it is narrow enough to answer. They can teach the method - how to control a variable, how to evaluate a source, how to handle uncertainty, how to structure an argument. They can read what the student has written and say where it falls short of the descriptor and why.

Outside the boundary is anything that results in words the student did not produce. A tutor does not supply paragraphs, does not rewrite a draft into its final form, and does not provide material to be submitted under the student's name. Stated like that it sounds restrictive; in practice the inside of that line is where nearly all the available improvement sits, because a student who can audit their own draft against a descriptor keeps that skill for the next one.

The same applies to materials. Subject guides, past papers, mark schemes and grade boundaries belong to the IB and the examination boards. A tutor references them and points to the official source rather than distributing copies, and nobody has access to unreleased papers or live boundaries. A claim to the contrary is a claim that cannot be true, and it should end the conversation.

sections.heading: Choosing between Maths AA and AI, and why it is a university decision
paragraphs: Two mathematics courses, four routes once level is included, and one of the most consequential choices a Diploma student makes in their first weeks. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and proof-oriented course; Applications and Interpretation emphasises modelling, statistics and the graphical calculator. Both run at Standard and Higher Level, and both carry the exploration at 20%.

The decision should be driven by the degree the student is aiming at rather than by which course looks easier. Engineering, mathematics, physics and many economics courses commonly expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and a student who takes Applications and Interpretation instead can find the prerequisite closed after results. Life sciences, psychology, business and design courses are usually content with either, and some explicitly welcome the statistics content in Applications and Interpretation.

The trap is the downgrade made for comfort in the first term. Moving from Analysis and Approaches Higher Level to Standard Level is a normal and often sensible decision when the student is drowning, but it should be made with a university list in front of you, checked against the published entry requirements of the courses on it, not on the basis of one bad test. Entry requirements vary by institution and change, so check each one directly.

Where a student is in the wrong course and the deadline for changing has passed, the response is a plan rather than a panic: identify the three topics carrying the most marks, build fluency there first, and use the exploration to secure a clean 20% while the papers are being rebuilt. That triage is one of the clearest uses of a weekly session in the first Diploma year.

sections.heading: Equivalency, attestation and what the Diploma has to show
paragraphs: Families in Umm Al Quwain looking at UAE universities will meet equivalency, a Ministry documentation process that almost no tutoring page mentions. It is worth understanding early, because subject choices made in the first Diploma year can affect it, and because it is a process a family manages rather than something a tutor performs.

For the British track the reported requirements are specific: one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, plus a pass in five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count. For the American track, English is reported as IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT 450 in reading and writing, with SAT Math at 450 or above required for mathematics.

For the IB there is no points figure published in that same reporting, which means any page quoting an IB equivalency threshold is quoting something unsourced. The correct answer to a parent asking is that the Ministry of Education or the relevant attestation authority is the only place to confirm it, and that it should be confirmed before decisions are made rather than after results arrive.

Two further things are worth saying clearly. Tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, university admission or school progression, and anybody presenting it that way is manufacturing urgency about a regulatory process. And IB Gram does not perform, submit or guarantee equivalency or attestation for anybody; the official channel is the Ministry's own, and that is where a family should go.

process.title: Send the subject, the level and the last report
process.description: Start with the subject, whether it is Higher or Standard Level, and if possible a recent marked piece of work or report. For a Diploma student the school's internal deadline list is the single most useful attachment, because the plan is built around it rather than around a generic IB year.

process.title: A free trial session with the tutor who would teach
process.description: The trial is a working session, not a sales call. The tutor sets a short diagnostic, marks a piece of the student's writing against the criteria or mark scheme, and gives a view on where marks are going. You see the match and the marking style before anything is agreed.

process.title: A written plan split between internal and external marks
process.description: After the trial the plan separates Internal Assessment work from paper work, because they fail differently and have different deadlines. It says what is covered in each block, what is set between sessions, and what is realistically reachable in the time before the session the student is entered for.

process.title: Weekly sessions with marked work returned
process.description: A fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time, one-to-one over live video, with a short task set each week and returned marked against the published criteria. The marking names the specific marks lost rather than writing a grade at the top, so a parent can read the script and see the issue.

process.title: Review at six weeks and change if nothing has moved
process.description: Six weeks produces enough marked evidence to judge whether the arrangement is working. If it is not, the right answer is a different tutor or a different plan, decided then. A change request is treated as a normal part of the arrangement rather than a complaint.

whyPoints.title: The marking explained, not just the content
whyPoints.description: Most Diploma marks are lost to mechanics: a command term misread, a criterion misunderstood, a conclusion never reached. Sessions start from the student's own marked work and name the specific losses, because that is the fastest available improvement and it transfers across subjects.

whyPoints.title: A slot that survives the commute
whyPoints.description: With most students travelling out of the emirate for school, the usable evening is short. Nothing travels to a live video session, so the hour is spent teaching rather than parked on the Sharjah road, and the weekly time holds through a full term.

whyPoints.title: Internal Assessment work kept on the right side of the line
whyPoints.description: Criteria explained, research questions discussed, method taught, drafts read against descriptors - with every assessed word produced by the student. That boundary is stated up front, because the alternative sold elsewhere in this market puts the qualification itself at risk.

whyPoints.title: Specialists matched by subject and level
whyPoints.description: Higher Level Chemistry and Standard Level Chemistry are different teaching jobs, and in a small emirate neither specialist is likely to live nearby. Online delivery removes geography from the match, so the tutor is chosen for the course the student actually sits.

whyPoints.title: Plans built on the school's own deadlines
whyPoints.description: Students here attend schools in other emirates, each with its own internal deadlines, mock weeks and draft dates. The tutoring plan is written from that list, so Internal Assessment work lands before the school's deadline rather than before a generic one.

whyPoints.title: A free trial before any commitment
whyPoints.description: The first session is free and is with the tutor who would teach. You see the diagnostic, the marking and the manner before deciding, which is a more useful basis for a decision than a profile page or a claim about results.

faqs.question: What does an IB tutor actually do that my child's school teacher cannot?
faqs.answer: A school teacher is teaching a class to a syllabus on a timetable. A tutor works from your child's own marked scripts and drafts, which means the diagnosis is specific: this criterion, this command term, this topic. In a one-to-one session the student has to answer out loud and cannot sit behind the class, so gaps surface in minutes rather than at the next assessment. The other difference is the Internal Assessment, where a tutor can take the time to go through each criterion descriptor against the student's own draft, line by line.

faqs.question: How are the 45 Diploma points made up?
faqs.answer: Six subjects each graded 1 to 7 give up to 42 points, and up to 3 more come from the matrix combining the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge grades, for a maximum of 45. Creativity, Activity, Service carries no points but must be completed. The Diploma requires at least 24 points together with several further conditions, so a student near the threshold should look at the conditions rather than only the total. Those conditions are where an otherwise passing total can still fail, which makes them worth checking with the school's coordinator early.

faqs.question: How much of my child's IB grade comes from the Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: In most subjects it is around a fifth of the final grade, and in some it is higher at Standard Level than at Higher Level. It is produced at school, marked by the teacher against published criteria and then moderated by the IB. The reason it matters more than its weight suggests is timing: the deadline falls well before the examinations, it cannot be resat the way a paper can, and the criteria are published, so a student can audit their own draft against the top descriptor before submitting it.

faqs.question: My child understands the subject but keeps scoring 4s. What is going wrong?
faqs.answer: Usually the shape of the answers rather than the knowledge. IB questions are built from command terms, and each one sets the depth expected. A student who describes when the term says evaluate scores in the lower band even when everything written is accurate, and a student who writes a paragraph for a term asking them to state loses the time they need later. This pattern is diagnosable from any marked script in about twenty minutes, and it is the most efficient thing to fix because it transfers across every subject at once.

faqs.question: Does anyone come to our home in Umm Al Quwain for lessons?
faqs.answer: No. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and home visits are a service offered only in India. There is no IB Gram centre or office in the UAE. In this emirate that format is the practical one anyway: most Diploma students commute out to Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah for school, the usable evening is short, and an arrangement that also requires somebody to drive into Umm Al Quwain spends the same scarce window on travel and tends to collapse in a busy term.

faqs.question: Which IB subjects do Umm Al Quwain families most often ask for?
faqs.answer: Mathematics in both courses, then Chemistry and Physics at Higher Level, then English A and Economics. The pattern reflects what a small emirate cannot staff deeply: a student at Higher Level in a subject with few local candidates often has nobody nearby to ask. Requests also cluster around the Internal Assessment season and around the first Diploma year, when students who did well in the Middle Years Programme meet external paper marking for the first time and find it rewards something different.

faqs.question: Which IB maths course should a student aiming at engineering be entered for?
faqs.answer: Let the degree decide, not the perceived difficulty. Analysis and Approaches is the algebra and proof course and is commonly expected at Higher Level for engineering, mathematics, physics and many economics degrees. Applications and Interpretation emphasises modelling and statistics and is usually acceptable for life sciences, psychology, business and design. Both carry the exploration at 20% of the grade. Check the published entry requirements of the specific courses on your child's list, because they vary by institution and change, and make any downgrade decision with that list in front of you.

faqs.question: What is the Extended Essay word limit, and how much help is allowed?
faqs.answer: The Extended Essay has a 4,000-word limit and is supervised at school. A tutor can explain the assessment criteria, discuss the research question until it is narrow enough to answer, teach the method of evaluating sources, and read a draft the student has written to say where it falls short of a descriptor. What nobody may do is supply paragraphs, rewrite the draft into final form, or provide text submitted under the student's name. The essay and Theory of Knowledge together carry up to 3 Diploma points, and most students gain them from a clear question rather than from extra words.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a Diploma student here usually start with?
faqs.answer: One subject, once a week, is the usual starting point, and it is the right one for most families. The commute from this emirate leaves a short evening, and two sessions on the same night produce less than one session plus completed work between them. Students in the final year with two weak subjects sometimes run two slots on different evenings, and in the weeks before a session the frequency rises. Starting small also makes the six-week review honest, because there is a clean record of what one weekly hour actually moved.

faqs.question: Can sessions be timed around a long bus commute to Sharjah or Ajman?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the timing should be designed rather than assumed. Students leaving Al Salamah or Al Raas early and arriving home between four and five in the afternoon do better with a six or seven o'clock slot, one subject only, with the hardest subject earlier rather than later because attention falls away after a long day. Children attending school in Ras Al Khaimah from Al Humrah are often home sooner and can take 4.30pm. The slot is set in Gulf Standard Time and kept fixed, since the tutor may be in another time zone.

faqs.question: Will the Ramadan timetable disrupt our weekly session in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: Families commonly move them later, after Iftar, and shorten them from ninety minutes to sixty, with a lighter load in the first week while the household adjusts. Because lessons are delivered over live video there is no travel to schedule around, so the shift is a conversation rather than a logistical problem. The useful thing is to plan it in advance: the examination calendar does not move for Ramadan, so a student who drifts for three weeks has to find those weeks again later, usually at the point when revision is already heaviest.

faqs.question: What does the first session produce, and what should I expect to see?
faqs.answer: A diagnostic rather than a lesson. The tutor sets a short set of questions across the syllabus areas, marks a piece of the student's own writing against the criteria or mark scheme, and gives a written view on where the marks are currently going - which command terms, which criteria, which topics. You should be able to read that without a teaching background. What you should not expect is a prediction of a grade; no honest tutor offers one, and a plan that names the weaknesses is worth more than one that names a number.

faqs.question: Who regulates private schools in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: The federal Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools in Umm Al Quwain, as it does in Ajman and Fujairah. Dubai has KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain have ADEK, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge. This matters for a family here because many students attend school in Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah, which puts them under that emirate's authority - and in Sharjah and RAK the authority also approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods.

faqs.question: Is private tutoring in the UAE regulated, and should I check anything?
faqs.answer: Yes. Paid private tutoring runs through a work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so any amount quoted to you online is unverified. Ask a tutor directly whether they hold it.

faqs.question: Does my child need tutoring to get UAE equivalency for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: No, and anybody suggesting otherwise is manufacturing urgency about a documentation process. Equivalency is handled by the Ministry of Education and the relevant attestation authority, and a family deals with them directly. Reported requirements are specific for the British and American tracks, but no IB points threshold appears in that reporting, so any page publishing one is quoting something unsourced. Confirm the current rules with the Ministry before making subject decisions, and note that IB Gram does not perform, submit or guarantee equivalency or attestation for anybody.

umm-al-quwain/ib-tutor.closingBody: The quickest way to find out whether an IB tutor will help your child is to put a piece of their marked work in front of one. Send the subject, the level and a recent script or Internal Assessment draft, and we will arrange a free trial session, one-to-one over live video, with the tutor who would actually teach. In that hour you should learn which command terms are costing marks, which criteria are being misread, and what is realistically reachable before the session your child is entered for. Then decide. No tutor can promise a grade; a good one can tell you precisely what is going wrong.

intro.heading: Why "near me" is the wrong first filter here
paragraphs: A parent searching for a tutor near them is doing something sensible for almost every other service. For a plumber, proximity is quality: the nearest competent one arrives soonest and charges least for getting there. For IB tuition in Umm Al Quwain, proximity does the opposite. It shrinks a small pool to a tiny one and then charges you for the privilege, because whoever is nearest is also whoever has to be paid to drive.

Start with the arithmetic that local searches hide. Umm Al Quwain is the least populous emirate. Most of the students here sitting the Diploma attend school in Sharjah, Ajman or Ras Al Khaimah, so the subject teachers who know those courses live where those schools are. The tutoring market a search for "near me" is drawing on is roughly an hour down the Emirates Road in ordinary traffic, which means a one-hour booking costs the tutor two hours of driving. That is paid for somewhere: in the rate, in a two-hour minimum, or in the reliability of the slot.

Now the prices, because almost nobody in this market publishes them. Three of the six pages ranking for UAE tutoring queries carry no figure at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not the currency a family here transacts in. This page quotes the market in dirhams and names where each figure came from. These are market bands compiled from providers' own published rates and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost table - they are not IB Gram's price list, and the honest answer to what IB Gram charges begins with a free trial lesson and a conversation about what the student actually needs.

Six things move the number in this emirate, and they are worth knowing before any call: the level, the subject's scarcity, the format, the session length, how close the examination session is, and whether travel is involved. A quote that moves AED 150 an hour between two providers usually has four of those six behind it, not a difference in quality. The sections below take each one apart.

One thing no quote should include is a promised result. There are no grade guarantees in any honest version of this service, and a rate justified by a claimed improvement is justified by something nobody can evidence. What a rate should buy is specific and checkable: a diagnosis, work set and marked between sessions, and an hour taught by somebody who has used the mark scheme for the course in question.

Delivery here is one-to-one over live video, and IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in the UAE; home visits are offered only in India, and there is no UAE office or centre. The relevant consequence for cost is simple: nothing is charged for travel because nothing travels, and the specialist can be matched to the student's actual course rather than to a postcode. For a student in Al Salamah entered for Higher Level Chemistry, that is the difference between a specialist and whatever is nearby.
