sections.heading: The June and November series, counted backwards
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes an exam calendar, which is odd, because it is the most actionable thing a parent can be handed. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series. UAE candidates sit those two. The February/March series is offered to India only, so any page quoting a March window to an Al Raas family is quoting another country's calendar.

Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. The zone belongs to the centre, which for most Al Raas students is a school in Ajman or Sharjah. Ask the exams officer which zone applies before planning anything around a published start time.

For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, exams run in May/June and in November. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those backward-looking dates establish the shape: a November series means results in January, which matters if a sixth-form or university application is in train. Pearson publishes provisional timetables and revises them, so work from the live official timetable rather than from dates restated anywhere else.

Read the table below as a chain rather than a list. Each row depends on the one above it, and the rows that bite hardest are the school-set ones near the top, which fall months before the papers and are the ones families routinely miss.

sections.heading: Where the exams are actually sat, and what a private candidate is
paragraphs: Most Al Raas students sit their papers at their own school, which is usually in Ajman or Sharjah. The school is the centre, the centre holds the zone allocation, and the entries are made by the exams officer. That arrangement is simple and it is the one almost every family is in.

It becomes complicated in three situations. A student who wants a subject the school does not offer has to find a centre that accepts private candidates. A student who has left school mid-course and wants to complete a qualification is in the same position. And a student resitting a single subject after a disappointing result may find their own school unwilling to enter them for one paper. In each case the entry is made with a centre that accepts external candidates, the fees are paid directly, and the deadlines are the centre's rather than the school's.

Two things to understand before going down that route. First, practical and coursework components are the hard part: a subject with a school-assessed component cannot always be taken as a private candidate, and the alternative-to-practical route exists precisely because of this. Check the subject, not just the board. Second, the deadlines for private entry are earlier and less forgiving than a school's internal reminders, because nobody is chasing you.

We do not arrange exam entries, hold a centre number or administer any board's examinations, and no tutoring provider should imply otherwise. What a tutor can do is teach the specification, prepare the student for the specific papers they will sit, and make sure the preparation matches the tier and board the entry was actually made for. Checking that match is worth doing in the first session rather than in March.

sections.heading: Five IGCSE passes: what the Ministry of Education counts
paragraphs: An Al Raas student finishing IGCSEs and applying to a UAE institution meets the Ministry of Education's equivalency process, which converts a foreign school certificate into something UAE universities and employers can read. Understanding it in Year 10 rather than after results day is worth real money, because it constrains subject choices while they can still be changed.

The published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, together with either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. That last detail catches families repeatedly, and at least one ranking competitor page publishes a six-subject requirement, which is simply wrong.

There is a tier consequence hiding in that rule. A Core-tier pass at grade C or D counts towards the five exactly as a pass does, so the equivalency floor is not the reason to push a student into Extended. The reason to push for Extended is a degree course that asks for higher grades or a specific subject at A-Level. Separating those two questions stops families making the tier decision for the wrong reason.

Two cautions. Equivalency is a Ministry process. IB Gram does not perform it, expedite it or guarantee an outcome in it, and we point you to the official channel rather than offering to handle it. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression; any provider implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency around a regulatory process.

The pool narrows to those willing to drive to Al Raas, which in a specific board and tier may be nobody. The rate carries the drive: the in-home band at AED 180 to 500 an hour overlaps the specialist band, but a share of the money is paying for the road rather than for specification knowledge. And the appointment has to be fixed against a bus arrival from Ajman or Sharjah that cannot be predicted to the quarter hour.

Online delivery handles each of those differently. The pool is everyone who teaches Cambridge 0620 Extended. The rate pays only for teaching. A late bus costs ten minutes rather than an hour and a wasted journey. Past papers screen-share and annotate live, mark schemes can be worked line by line, and the session can be recorded and rewatched the night before a paper, which a kitchen-table lesson never produces.

IB Gram offers only the online route in the UAE. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. sections.heading: Where IGCSE marks are lost, and what a tutor can actually fix
paragraphs: Most IGCSE underperformance is not a content gap. It is a mark-scheme gap. A student who understands moles and loses marks for an unbalanced equation, or who can do the physics and loses marks for omitting units, is not short of knowledge. They are short of the specific habits the scheme rewards, and those habits are among the fastest things in education to install.

The diagnosis has to come from marked papers rather than from a conversation. Take four or five past papers, mark them against the official scheme, and sort the lost marks by cause: content not known, method not shown, command term misread, units or notation, time ran out. The distribution is almost always lopsided, and it tells you what the next six sessions should contain. Most families have never seen their child's losses sorted this way.

What responds quickly: showing working so method marks survive a wrong final answer; reading the command term and answering that verb rather than the topic; using the right number of significant figures; labelling diagrams; and in the sciences, describing apparatus and method with the precision the practical papers demand. What responds slowly: two years of missing algebra. A tutor who promises the second in six weeks is selling you something.

For an Al Raas student the practical value of this is time. There are fewer usable weekday hours in a commuting household, so the hours must be spent on the highest-yield losses rather than on a general sweep through the syllabus. Sorting the losses first is how a small number of sessions does disproportionate work.

faqs.question: Can we find an IGCSE home tutor in Al Raas or should we look wider?
faqs.answer: Looking wider inside Umm Al Quwain adds very little, because the constraint is the size of the emirate rather than your position in it. Al Riqqa, Al Salamah and UAQ Marina draw on the same small pool. What does change the outcome is narrowing by specification instead: Cambridge 0580 Extended or Pearson 4MA1, with the tier named. That filter finds a tutor who can lift a grade, and because we deliver over live video, where they live stops mattering.

The market does supply in-home tutors at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour on published 2026 figures, with the drive inside that rate. In Umm Al Quwain the drive is long and the pool willing to make it for a specific board and tier is very small.

faqs.question: Is Core or Extended the right entry for a borderline student?
faqs.answer: Decide it on timed evidence rather than classwork. Core is capped at grade C; Extended reaches A*. A capable student entered for Core is capped for two years, and an unready student entered for Extended can score below their Core potential. Three or four sessions of Extended-standard past-paper questions under proper timing, marked against the official scheme, produce a defensible answer. Schools listen to that kind of evidence because it is the kind they use themselves.

faqs.question: How do I find out which exam board my child is actually doing?
faqs.answer: Look at the statement of entry, or ask the exams officer directly. You are looking for a code: Cambridge 0580, 0625, 0620, 0610, or Pearson 4MA1, 4PH1, 4CH1, 4BI1. For Cambridge you also want the tier. Those few characters determine which papers your child sits, how the marks are awarded and therefore which tutor is the right one. A provider who does not ask for the code before quoting is telling you something useful.

faqs.question: We moved schools mid-course and the board changed. What now?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a real transition rather than a formality. Cambridge and Pearson differ in paper structure, tiering, calculator rules and how practical skills are assessed, so a student halfway through 0580 arriving at a 4MA1 cohort has specific gaps rather than general weakness. A few focused sessions on the differences, working from the new specification and its past papers, closes most of it. Ask the new school in writing which code and tier they intend to enter your child for.

faqs.question: Which series will my child sit in the UAE?
faqs.answer: For Cambridge, the June series or the November series. The February/March series is offered to India only, so ignore any page quoting a March window to a UAE family. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and in November. Cambridge also allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version and warns that a wrong-zone miss is the candidate's own risk, so ask your school's exams officer which zone the centre sits in.

faqs.question: When do November results come out?
faqs.answer: For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE the pattern is January: November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For the June series, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Those are past dates, cited so you can see the shape rather than relied on for a future series. Pearson publishes and revises provisional timetables, so take exact dates from the live official timetable rather than from any page restating them.

faqs.question: Can my child sit an IGCSE as a private candidate?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the subject matters more than the board. A qualification with a school-assessed practical or coursework component cannot always be taken privately, which is why alternative-to-practical papers exist. You would need a centre that accepts external candidates, and the entry deadlines are earlier and less forgiving than a school's internal reminders because nobody chases you. IB Gram is not an exam centre and does not make entries; your school's exams officer is the place to start.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does the Ministry of Education count?
faqs.answer: Five. The published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus either one A-Level subject at E or two AS-Level subjects at E. At least one ranking competitor page states six, which is incorrect. Equivalency is a Ministry process that IB Gram does not perform or guarantee, so verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: Does a Core-tier grade still count towards equivalency?
faqs.answer: A pass at no less than grade E or grade 3 counts, and a Core-tier pass meets that standard, so the equivalency floor is not a reason to push a student into Extended. The reason to aim for Extended is a degree course asking for higher grades or a specific A-Level subject that needs the Extended content as a foundation. Separating those two questions stops families making the tier decision for the wrong reason, which happens often.

faqs.question: What does an IGCSE tutor charge in this part of the UAE?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market rates read in October 2026 put a qualified subject tutor online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150, and budget online tutoring from around AED 45. In-home visits run AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure. Monthly, Bestimate estimates AED 600 to 1,200 for a weekly hour with a qualified tutor. Umm Al Quwain is not separately surveyed; treat the national bands as a guide, and these are market figures rather than ours.

faqs.question: My child knows the content but the marks do not show it. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always a mark-scheme gap rather than a knowledge gap. Marks go on working shown, command terms answered, units given, significant figures right and diagrams labelled, and a student can understand a topic thoroughly while losing marks on all five. The fix is to mark four or five past papers against the official scheme and sort the losses by cause. The distribution is usually lopsided, and it tells you exactly what the next few sessions should contain.

faqs.question: Is a permit required to tutor privately in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring is regulated through a MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so be sceptical of any specific amount quoted at you.

faqs.question: Who regulates the school my Al Raas child attends in Ajman?
faqs.answer: The federal Ministry of Education, which supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. If the school is in Sharjah instead, the Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates it and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods. Dubai has KHDA and Abu Dhabi has ADEK. The practical point is that the regulator follows the school rather than your home address, so fee and curriculum questions go wherever the school sits.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover Maths and Physics for the same IGCSE student?
faqs.answer: Often yes, because the overlap in algebraic technique and in the style of multi-step problem is substantial, and a single specialist can handle both well at this level. Chemistry and Biology sit further apart than they look. Across two different boards the case weakens quickly, because specification knowledge is the thing being bought. Our default for an exam-year student is one specialist per subject unless the overlap is genuinely strong, and we will say which case applies.

umm-al-quwain/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-riq.tutorsIntro: These profiles are the IGCSE specialists Al Riqqa families most often need: Maths across both boards, the three separate sciences, English Language, and the Business and Economics pair that small cohorts rarely staff twice.

intro.heading: The question behind the search: who has actually taught this specification?
paragraphs: A parent in Al Riqqa does not really want a tutor who lives nearby. They want somebody who has taught their child's exact course and can say, without looking it up, where candidates lose marks on it. Proximity is a proxy people use because search engines offer it. The proxy is poor, and in a small emirate it is actively misleading.

Start with what the course actually is. "IGCSE Maths" is not one qualification. Cambridge 0580 is tiered into Core, capped at grade C, and Extended, reaching A*. Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 is untiered and awards 9 to 1. The papers are structured differently, the calculator rules differ, and the mark schemes reward different things. The same is true across the subjects: 0625 and 4PH1 in Physics, 0620 and 4CH1 in Chemistry, 0610 and 4BI1 in Biology. A tutor who has taught one of a pair is competent on the other and slightly out of position, and at the top of the grade range slightly out of position is the whole difference.

Now the supply question, answered honestly. Umm Al Quwain is the least populous emirate. Its private international school set is small, and most internationally schooled students from Al Riqqa commute out to Ajman, Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah. Specialist teachers exist roughly in proportion to the number of students sitting a specification, so the number of people within a short drive of Al Riqqa who have taken cohorts through Cambridge 0620 Extended is small. For the less commonly taught subjects it is often nobody at all, at any price.

That is not a counsel of despair, because the constraint is local supply rather than supply. Somewhere there are teachers who have taught 0620 Extended for five years and know that the moles questions and the Paper 6 apparatus descriptions are where the marks go. IB Gram matches your child to one of them and runs the session over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. The market does supply in-home visits at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour on published 2026 figures, with the drive inside the rate, and this page gives you those numbers rather than hiding them.

The rest of the page is built to make you a harder customer. There is a subject-by-subject account of where local supply runs out, the three questions that identify a genuine specialist in under a minute, what the market charges and who published each figure, the June and November series with the administrative-zone rule that catches families out, a breakdown of where IGCSE marks are really lost, the regulator map, and the five IGCSE passes the Ministry of Education counts towards equivalency.

programmes.name: Years 7 to 9, before the specification begins
programmes.description: Nothing is externally assessed yet, so specification knowledge matters least here and general teaching quality matters most. The things being built are algebraic fluency, reading stamina and the ability to write a structured explanation, and all three decide IGCSE grades two or three years later.
programmes.countryNote: For an Al Riqqa family this is the one stage where a local generalist is genuinely a reasonable choice, because there is no syllabus to know yet. It is also the cheapest and least used intervention: fixing number fluency in Year 8 costs a fraction of repairing it in Year 11, when a specialist is needed and the clock is running.

programmes.name: Year 10, the first IGCSE year
programmes.description: Roughly half the specification is taught and the Cambridge tier decision is made. Core and Extended diverge here, and the choice sets the grade ceiling for two years. In the sciences the practical skills work begins properly, and in Maths the algebra the final papers depend on is introduced.
programmes.countryNote: Specification knowledge starts to matter in Year 10, and this is the stage at which the local pool begins to fail an Al Riqqa family. A tutor who does not know whether your child is on 0580 Core, 0580 Extended or 4MA1 cannot give useful advice on the tier decision, and the tier decision is the most consequential one of the year.

programmes.name: Year 11, the exam year
programmes.description: Specification completion plus past-paper technique, and most of the available marks sit in the second. Mark schemes reward specific wording, specific working and specific units, so a student who knows the content but not the scheme loses method marks on every paper. Alternative-to-practical papers reward apparatus precision theory revision never supplies.
programmes.countryNote: This is where only a specialist will do, and where the local pool in Umm Al Quwain is thinnest. An Al Riqqa Year 11 student sits their papers at their school's centre, usually in Ajman or Sharjah, which carries its own Cambridge administrative zone and therefore its own timetable version.

umm-al-quwain/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-riq.subjectsIntro: The IGCSE subjects Al Riqqa families ask for, with the codes and the specific places candidates lose marks. Ask any prospective tutor to do the same from memory.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Extended reaches A* and Core stops at C, making the tier the biggest decision of Year 10. Marks go on transformations, bounds, and the last part of multi-step problems where method marks were available for working the student never wrote down.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Electricity is the predictable collapse topic, and the alternative-to-practical paper punishes students who have read about circuits but never described a workable method. Pearson's paper structure and formula-sheet treatment differ from Cambridge's, which is exactly why the code matters.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Moles calculations and organic naming carry the marks. Cambridge 0620 Paper 6 rewards precision about apparatus, observation and safety that no textbook summary supplies. Unbalanced equations cost marks in questions the student otherwise answered correctly.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Looks like recall, is marked like precision. Command terms decide the mark: describe, explain, suggest and compare each want a different answer shape. Enzymes, transport in plants and genetics are where timed performance usually collapses.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Reading questions are marked against specific skills rather than general comprehension, and directed writing is assessed on audience and form as much as content. A fluent writer who ignores the stated purpose of the task loses marks that have nothing to do with their English.

subjects.name: Business Studies
subjects.description: The case study decides the grade. Candidates who revise definitions and ignore the stimulus write generic answers and lose the high-tariff marks. Application to the named business is the assessed skill, and it is among the fastest improvements available at this level.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams carry marks and most candidates draw them carelessly: unlabelled axes, no shifted curve, no new equilibrium marked. Evaluation questions want a judgement supported by the analysis already written, not a fresh argument introduced in the final line.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode, trace tables and logic gates are mechanical marks thrown away for want of practice rather than understanding. Database and networking topics are taught thinly in small cohorts, which is precisely the shortage a commuting Umm Al Quwain student meets.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Taken by strong mathematicians heading for A-Level or the IB Diploma. Calculus, trigonometric identities and logarithms arrive early, and the step in algebraic demand from 0580 Extended is steeper in the first term than most students expect.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Federal rules require UAE private schools to teach Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies whatever curriculum they are licensed to deliver. Tutoring means supporting the school's own prescribed material, since different or additional content may not be used for mandatory subjects without Ministry permission.

sections.heading: Subject by subject, where the local supply runs out
paragraphs: Generic claims about tutor availability are useless, so here is the specific version. Specialist supply tracks the number of students sitting a specification. In a small emirate that means Maths and the three sciences are reasonably covered, because almost every candidate takes them, and everything else thins out fast.

Maths at both boards is the easiest to staff: every IGCSE student sits it, so every school has several teachers of it and some of them tutor. Physics, Chemistry and Biology follow, though the Cambridge and Pearson split halves each pool, and a family on 4CH1 cannot assume the local 0620 teacher is the right match. English Language is widely taught but unevenly tutored, because marking directed writing against the scheme is a specific skill that general English teaching does not confer.

Then the drop. Business Studies, Economics and Computer Science are taken by a fraction of a cohort, and in a school with a hundred IGCSE candidates that may be fifteen students and one teacher. If that teacher is unavailable, or cannot tutor students from their own school, there is no local second option. Additional Mathematics is rarer still. The mandatory UAE subjects sit in their own category, because tutoring them means supporting the school's prescribed material rather than teaching freely.

sections.heading: Three questions that identify a real IGCSE specialist in a minute
paragraphs: A parent cannot assess subject expertise directly, but they can assess it indirectly, and it takes less time than most people spend reading reviews. These three questions do almost all the work, and a genuine specialist answers all three without hesitation or preparation.

First: which syllabus code and tier, and how many cohorts have you taken through it? The answer should be a number and a code: five cohorts of 0580 Extended, three of 4MA1. Vagueness here is the whole answer. Second: which paper do candidates reliably lose marks on in this specification, and why? A specialist names a paper and a failure mode in one sentence — Paper 6 apparatus descriptions, Paper 4 multi-step working, electricity in Paper 2. Somebody who has not taught it redirects to their degree subject or their years of experience in education generally.

Third, and most revealing: what would you ask me for before the first session? The right answer is the statement of entry or the exam entry slip, so they can confirm the code and tier, plus any marked work. A tutor who does not ask for the code is planning to teach the subject rather than the specification, and at the top of the grade range those are different jobs.

A fourth question is worth adding where a tutor claims examiner status: can you evidence that it is current? Examiner claims are unverifiable from a website and are often used to imply access to marking standards, boundaries or paper content that nobody outside the process has. We do not describe tutors as examiners unless the status can be evidenced, and we never use it to imply access of that kind.

sections.heading: Why a small cohort cannot staff a specification twice
paragraphs: The supply problem in Umm Al Quwain is structural rather than accidental, and understanding the mechanism saves a family from assuming they have searched badly. Schools staff subjects in proportion to enrolment. A school with a hundred IGCSE candidates needs several Maths teachers and perhaps one Business Studies teacher. A school with three hundred needs three.

Private tutors are drawn from that same population, which is why tutoring supply mirrors school staffing and why it is lumpy rather than smooth. There is no mechanism by which a neighbourhood produces a Computer Science 0478 specialist in the absence of students taking 0478. Searching harder within the emirate does not create one. This is also why the pages for Al Riqqa, Al Raas, Al Salamah and UAQ Marina honestly give the same answer: they are drawing on one small pool.

There is a second constraint on top of the first. A school's own teacher is often not available to tutor the school's own students. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. So the one local specialist your child's school employs may be exactly the person who cannot help.

The way out is to stop treating the emirate as the market. The pool of people who have taught Cambridge 0455 Economics is national and international, and a live video lesson reaches all of it. That is the whole of the argument, and it is stronger here than almost anywhere in the UAE precisely because the local pool is so small.

Before accepting a quote, ask whether it is per hour or per session, whether it includes VAT, what a cancellation inside 24 hours costs, whether the rate rises before a series, and what happens if the tutor turns out to teach a different board. sections.heading: June, November and the zone rule nobody mentions
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. UAE candidates sit June and November. The February/March series is offered to India only, so a page quoting a March exam window to an Al Riqqa family is quoting a different country's calendar, and that is a date a parent would act on.

The part almost nobody publishes is the zone rule. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and says plainly that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. The zone belongs to the centre. For an Al Riqqa student the centre is almost certainly their school in Ajman or Sharjah, so the right question for the exams officer is which zone the centre sits in — not which timetable turned up in a search.

For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, exams run in May/June and in November. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those past dates establish the pattern — a November series means January results — which matters if a sixth-form or university application is in train. Pearson publishes provisional timetables and revises them, so take exact dates from the live official timetable.

sections.heading: What a specialist does that a generalist cannot
paragraphs: This is the practical core of the supply argument. If a generalist and a specialist both understand the topic, why does the specialist produce a different grade? Because most IGCSE underperformance is not a knowledge gap. It is a mark-scheme gap, and mark schemes are specification-specific.

A specialist knows that Cambridge 0620 Paper 6 wants apparatus named, a method that would actually work, and an observation that could actually be seen, and that vague competence scores nothing there. They know that 0580 Extended awards method marks for working a student can be trained to always write down. They know which command terms recur in which paper and what each one demands. A generalist teaching the same topic teaches the chemistry, which the student may already have, and leaves the marks on the table.

The diagnosis has to come from marked papers rather than from conversation. Take four or five past papers, mark them against the official scheme, and sort every lost mark by cause: content not known, method not shown, command term misread, units or notation, time ran out. The distribution is almost always lopsided, and it tells you precisely what the next six sessions should contain. Most families have never seen their child's losses sorted this way, and the sorting is the cheapest useful thing available.

What responds fast: showing working so method marks survive a wrong answer; answering the command term rather than the topic; significant figures; labelled diagrams; apparatus precision in the practical papers. What responds slowly: two years of missing algebra. Anyone promising the second inside six weeks is selling you something, and a specialist will tell you which category your child is in.

sections.heading: The regulator map, and the approval nobody holds
paragraphs: Al Riqqa sits in Umm Al Quwain, where private schools are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, as they are in Ajman and Fujairah. Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, activities and assessment methods. Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge on the same model. Dubai has KHDA, responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, and Abu Dhabi has ADEK, which supervises licensing and accreditation of private schools. Those five bodies are the complete map.

A family here frequently lives under one and schools under another, which matters when a fee or curriculum question needs answering: the question follows the school rather than your address. It does not matter at all for tutoring, because none of those bodies licenses or approves individual tutors or tutoring platforms.

Tutoring is regulated separately. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers applicants including teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so this page quotes none, and any specific amount circulating should be treated as unverified. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time.

The consequence is a sentence worth being blunt about. No tutoring provider in this country can honestly describe itself as approved or accredited by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA or the Ministry of Education. A KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific licence issued to training institutes with premises in Dubai. IB Gram holds no such permit, no accreditation from any UAE authority, no partnership with Cambridge or Pearson, and is not an examination centre. We explain what each body does and link to it, which is the only honest use of those names.

sections.heading: Five IGCSE passes: the equivalency rule worth knowing in Year 10
paragraphs: An Al Riqqa student finishing IGCSEs and applying to a UAE institution meets the Ministry of Education's equivalency process, which converts a foreign school certificate into something UAE universities and employers can read. Knowing the rule in Year 10 rather than after results day is worth real money, because it constrains subject choices while they are still changeable.

The published British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, together with either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. At least one ranking competitor page publishes a six-subject requirement, which is incorrect, and a family planning against the wrong number makes a real mistake.

There is a tier consequence buried in that rule. A Core-tier pass at grade C or D meets the no-less-than-E standard, so the equivalency floor is not a reason to push a borderline student into Extended. The reason to aim for Extended is a degree course asking for higher grades or an A-Level subject that needs Extended content as its foundation. Separating those two questions stops the tier decision being made for the wrong reason, which happens often.

Two cautions. Equivalency is a Ministry process: IB Gram does not perform it, expedite it or guarantee an outcome, and we point you to the official channel rather than offering to handle it. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression. A provider implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency around a regulatory process.

sections.heading: What we say when the honest answer is no
paragraphs: Everything above leads to a commitment, and it is the part of this page we would most like a parent to hold us to. If no specialist in your child's board, code and tier is free in the hours an Al Riqqa school run leaves, we will say so rather than filling the slot.

That matters most in exactly the subjects this page has been honest about: Computer Science 0478, Additional Mathematics 0606, Economics and Business Studies on the less common of the two boards. In those cases the options are a different evening with the right person, a specialist based outside the UAE working to Gulf Standard Time, or a wait. We name which one applies. We do not substitute a competent generalist and let you discover in week three that your child is being taught the subject rather than the specification.

No competitor page examined for this project discloses a coverage limit anywhere, and several conceal non-UAE delivery behind a non-UAE phone number. If the specialist who fits your child is not based in the UAE, the lesson still runs over live video on your timetable and we tell you where they are before the first session rather than after it.

The matching conversation is short: the board code and tier from the statement of entry, the school and its assessment calendar, the two or three things the student keeps losing marks on, and the hours that work after the Ajman run. A free trial lesson follows, with no minimum booking attached, so you can judge the match rather than take our word for it. If the fit is wrong, say so in week one and we will change it.

faqs.question: Is there anyone near Al Riqqa who actually knows my child's IGCSE syllabus?
faqs.answer: For Maths and the three sciences, possibly: those subjects are taken by nearly every candidate so every school staffs them and some of those teachers tutor. For Business Studies, Economics, Computer Science or Additional Mathematics, usually not, because a small cohort supports one teacher rather than two. That is a structural feature of the least populous emirate, not a failure of your search. Matching on the syllabus code and teaching over live video solves it.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to Al Riqqa homes?
faqs.answer: No. We do not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. All UAE tuition is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The market does supply in-home tutors at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour on published 2026 figures, with the drive inside the rate. Al Riqqa is the shortest drive in the emirate from the Ajman corridor, so a local quote should sit at the lower end.

faqs.question: How do I check a tutor really knows the specification?
faqs.answer: Ask three things. Which syllabus code and tier, and how many cohorts have you taken through it. Which paper do candidates reliably lose marks on in this specification, and why. And what would you ask me for before the first session. A specialist answers with a code, a number, a named paper and a failure mode, and asks for the statement of entry. Anyone who redirects to their degree subject has told you what you needed to know.

faqs.question: Why can't my child's own teacher tutor them privately?
faqs.answer: Sometimes they can and often they may not. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. In a small emirate that means the one local specialist in a minority subject may be precisely the person who cannot help your child.

faqs.question: Does searching a wider area in Umm Al Quwain help?
faqs.answer: Barely. Al Raas, Al Salamah and UAQ Marina draw on the same small pool as Al Riqqa, because the constraint is the size of the emirate rather than your position inside it. The first real increase comes at the Ajman urban edge and the next in northern Sharjah, and a tutor travelling from there is charging you for the drive inside their hourly rate. Online delivery reaches the full pool without that cost.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE board is my child actually sitting?
faqs.answer: Check the statement of entry or ask the exams officer. You want a code: Cambridge 0580, 0625, 0620, 0610, or Pearson 4MA1, 4PH1, 4CH1, 4BI1. For Cambridge you also want the tier, Core or Extended. Those characters decide which papers your child sits, how marks are awarded and therefore which tutor fits. Cambridge and Pearson differ on tiering, paper structure, calculator rules and practical assessment, so the code is not a detail.

faqs.question: Which series do UAE candidates sit?
faqs.answer: Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit the June series and the November series. The February/March series is offered to India only, so disregard any page quoting a March window here. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and in November. Cambridge also allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version, and says it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who used the wrong one, so ask which zone your centre sits in.

faqs.question: Why does the timetable zone depend on the school rather than our address?
faqs.answer: Because the zone is allocated to the exam centre, and the centre is the school that enters your child. For an Al Riqqa family that is almost always a school in Ajman or Sharjah rather than anything in Umm Al Quwain. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone. The practical step is to ask the exams officer for the zone in writing, and then work from that version only.

faqs.question: My child understands the subject but the marks are low. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always a mark-scheme gap rather than a knowledge gap. Marks go on working shown, the command term answered, units given, significant figures correct and diagrams labelled, and a student can understand a topic thoroughly while losing marks on all five. The fix is to mark four or five past papers against the official scheme and sort every lost mark by cause. The distribution is usually lopsided and it tells you what the next sessions should contain.

faqs.question: What should IGCSE tuition cost in the northern emirates?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market rates read in October 2026 put a qualified subject tutor online at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150, and budget online tutoring from around AED 45. Code and tier specialists run AED 200 to 450 or more. In-home visits sit at AED 180 to 500 with the drive inside the figure. Monthly, Bestimate estimates AED 600 to 1,200 for a weekly hour with a qualified tutor.

faqs.question: Is Core or Extended the better entry for a student in the middle?
faqs.answer: Decide it on timed evidence rather than classwork, because both wrong answers are costly. Core caps the grade at C for two years; Extended entry for a student who cannot finish a paper under timing scores below their Core potential. Three or four sessions of Extended-standard past-paper questions under real timing, marked against the official scheme, produce a defensible conclusion. Schools listen to that because it is the same kind of evidence they use themselves.

faqs.question: Does a Core grade still count for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Ministry's British-track rule asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and a Core-tier pass meets that standard. So equivalency is not a reason to push a borderline student into Extended. The reason to aim for Extended is a degree course that asks for higher grades or an A-Level subject needing Extended content as its foundation. Verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor claim to be approved by the Ministry of Education?
faqs.answer: No, and the claim should end the conversation. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Umm Al Quwain, Ajman and Fujairah; KHDA, ADEK, SPEA and the RAK Department of Knowledge cover the other emirates. None of them approves or accredits tutors or tutoring platforms. A KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific licence for training institutes with premises in Dubai. IB Gram holds no such permit and no accreditation from any UAE authority.

faqs.question: What happens if nobody covers my child's subject at our hour?
faqs.answer: We tell you before you commit and name the options: a different evening with the right specialist, a specialist based outside the UAE working to Gulf Standard Time, or a wait. For subjects like Computer Science 0478 or Additional Mathematics 0606 the wait is sometimes the right answer. We do not substitute a competent generalist and let you discover in week three that your child is being taught the subject rather than the specification.

faqs.question: How late is too late to start before a series?
faqs.answer: Six weeks is late and still useful; two weeks is mostly triage. In six weeks a specialist can change how a student handles the question types losing them the most marks, fix working and notation habits, and make them faster under timing. What six weeks cannot do is install two years of missing content, and anyone saying otherwise is selling you something. The honest plan at that point is to pick three high-yield question types from marked evidence.

intro.heading: The calendar decides what an hour is worth
paragraphs: Al Salamah families arrive at this search at wildly different points in the year, and the same tutor doing the same good work produces very different value depending on which point that is. A Year 10 student in the autumn term has time to close content gaps and build habits. A Year 11 student in the spring has time to fix technique and protect reachable marks. A Year 11 student six weeks out has time to do one thing well. Treating those three as the same purchase is the main way money gets wasted on IGCSE tuition.

So the first question is not which subject but which series. Cambridge runs a June series and a November series for candidates in the UAE. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May or June and again in November. Your child's statement of entry names the series, the board, the subject codes and the papers, and it is the single most useful document in the house. Without it, a tutor is guessing, and guessing in April is expensive.

The second question is what the last honest mark was. School reports and predicted grades are useful but they are compressed, and they are often generous in the autumn and pessimistic after a bad mock. A timed paper marked strictly against the published mark scheme is the only document that tells you where the marks are actually going, and it takes one session to produce. Every plan on this page starts there.

The third question is how the weeks remaining should be shaped, and that is where most families get the arithmetic wrong in the same direction. Content work has to finish before paper work starts, because technique needs something to operate on. If there are twenty weeks, there is room for both. If there are eight, there is room for one, and the honest advice is usually to narrow the plan rather than add a second session.

There is a fourth question that families rarely ask and should. How many subjects are you actually buying? The arithmetic of a weekly hour is unforgiving: eight sessions plus the written work set between them is something like twenty to twenty-five hours of genuine effort. That quantity moves one subject properly, or makes partial progress in two. Spread across four it produces a tired candidate and four unchanged grades, which is the commonest outcome of a panic purchase in the spring term of Year 11. Choosing the one or two subjects where the marked scripts show recoverable marks is the whole discipline, and it is a decision the evidence should make rather than the anxiety.

Delivery, stated plainly: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE, and in-person visits are an India-only service. Al Salamah lessons happen one-to-one over live video, scheduled to Gulf Standard Time around the Sharjah or Ajman school run. That is also what allows the plan to start this week rather than whenever somebody is free to drive to Umm Al Quwain.

umm-al-quwain/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-sal.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Al Salamah families most often need under time pressure, with a note on how quickly each responds to focused work. That matters when there are eight weeks rather than eighty.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The fastest-responding subject in the set, because so many lost marks are method and presentation rather than understanding. Surds left unsimplified, bearings measured from the wrong line, probability trees never multiplied along the branch. Six focused sessions often move a grade.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Mechanics and electricity carry the marks and the losses. Responds well to short-window work if the diagnosis is accurate, because the recurring errors are units, graph reading and the describe-versus-explain confusion rather than missing content.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles and electrolysis need genuine content time, so this is a poor candidate for a six-week rescue if those topics are missing. Qualitative analysis and equation writing, by contrast, are drillable in a fortnight and worth real marks.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.description: Content-heavy, which makes it the slowest subject to rescue late but the most rewarding to work on through Year 10. Language precision is the lever: diffusion is not osmosis, and a cross needs its gametes shown before the ratio earns anything.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 / 0511)
subjects.description: The summary task with its strict word allowance is the single most improvable component in the whole subject, and it responds to practice within weeks. Extended writing takes longer because register is a habit rather than a technique.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500 / 0990)
subjects.description: Directed writing and composition, marked on structure and effect. Late work should target the directed task, which has a learnable shape, rather than the composition, which depends on a breadth of practice that cannot be built in a month.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450 / Edexcel 4BS1)
subjects.description: Command-term led, which makes it unusually responsive to short-window technique work. Students who know the content and write explain answers to evaluate questions are leaving a grade on the table and can recover it quickly.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy is pure technique and improves fast. Data-response discipline, quoting a figure from the extract for every claim, is a habit that takes three or four marked attempts to install and then holds.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478 / 0984)
subjects.description: Binary, hexadecimal and logic gates are quick wins available in any window. Pseudocode under timing takes longer, and trace tables are the component most often abandoned when a student is short of time, despite carrying available marks.

sections.heading: Where your child sits in the IGCSE year, and what is still changeable
paragraphs: The honest first conversation is about what time allows rather than what a tutor can teach. Content, technique and stamina need different quantities of time, and they do not substitute for each other. Twenty weeks can cover a content gap and then build technique on top of it. Eight weeks can build technique on content that already exists. Three weeks can rehearse timing and protect the marks a student already has access to, which is a smaller claim and sometimes the right one.

That framing also tells you what to decline. A tutor who, six weeks out from the papers, proposes starting at the beginning of the syllabus and working forward is proposing something that cannot finish. A tutor who proposes four hours a week in four different subjects in the final month is proposing something that will exhaust the student without concentrating anywhere. Both happen, and both are easier to refuse if you know which window you are in.

The corresponding mistake in Year 10 is the opposite one. Families with time available often wait, on the reasonable theory that there is no crisis yet. The structural problem is that roughly two-thirds of the examined content is taught in Year 10 and then left alone, so the Year 11 student who seems to have forgotten everything genuinely has. An hour a week of maintenance across Year 10 is the cheapest intervention in the qualification, and the one that is almost never bought.
The table below is the version of this a tutor uses on a first call. Find the row that matches your weeks remaining, and treat the last column as what to insist on rather than what to hope for.

sections.heading: The June series counted backwards from today
paragraphs: Exam-session awareness is the biggest single gap in the pages competing for this search: the word November barely appears on any of them, and no competitor names an entry deadline. That is a strange omission, because the deadlines are the only fixed points in the whole process and they all sit earlier than families expect.

Counting backwards is the right direction because the deadline nearest you is usually an internal one. The school's own cut-off for confirming entries and tiers sits before the board's final entry date, often by several weeks, and it is the one that actually binds your family. Tier decisions in Cambridge subjects, where Core caps the grade available, get locked at that point. If there is an argument to be had about Core versus Extended, it has to happen before the cut-off and not after the mock.

After entries, the mock window is the next fixed point and the last honest diagnostic. Then comes the content deadline, which nobody sets and which is the reason plans fail: content work must finish roughly eight weeks before the papers so that technique has a runway. A student still meeting new material three weeks out is not revising, they are learning, and the two feel similar and pay differently.

Pearson's published dates make a usable worked example because they are real and checkable. The November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also issues provisional timetables well ahead of each series, which is exactly why you should open the live official timetable rather than trust a date restated on any tutoring page, including this one.

sections.heading: The eight-week plan, week by week
paragraphs: Most students in the final two months do past papers, mark them kindly, feel briefly reassured and repeat. That trains very little. The plan below is slower, covers fewer papers and produces movement you can see on a mark scheme, and it is the structure a pre-series block here actually follows.

Week one is one timed paper, marked strictly, with every lost mark put into a category: content gap, command term misread, working not shown, or ran out of time. That single sheet is the diagnosis and it usually contradicts the student's own account of their weaknesses. Weeks two to five attack the biggest category in question-sized pieces, repeating the same question type until it stops failing, rather than moving through topics in syllabus order.

Weeks six and seven return to whole papers under real timing, including the sections the student would normally skip, because skipped sections are free marks left behind. Week eight is deliberately light: sleep, a short retrieval routine, and the practical business of knowing which papers fall on which day. A tired candidate loses more marks in the hall than an under-revised one, and the last week is the only variable still fully in your control.

The arithmetic to watch is total hours. Eight weekly sessions plus set written work between them is roughly twenty to twenty-five hours of focused effort. That is enough to fix technique in one subject or make real progress in two. It is not enough for four, and a plan that says otherwise is selling hours rather than marks.

sections.heading: What mocks really tell you, and what they do not
paragraphs: Mock results arrive with more authority than they deserve and get read for the wrong information. The grade is the least useful part. The paper itself, with the marks annotated question by question, is where the value is, and most families never ask for it. Ask. A school will usually release the script to a parent who requests a specific component rather than a general explanation.

What a mock reliably tells you is pattern. Which question types failed, whether the back half of the paper was reached, whether the long-answer marks were taken, whether units and working were present. Those are the things that transfer directly to the real series, because they are habits rather than knowledge.

What a mock does not tell you is the final grade. Mock papers are often older papers, marked by teachers against their own boundary estimates, sat in a hall with a different atmosphere and sometimes before the syllabus has finished. A mock grade below the target is not a prediction; it is a snapshot with known distortions. Equally, a comfortable mock grade on an incomplete syllabus is not reassurance.

The useful response to a disappointing mock is therefore narrow and quick: get the script, categorise the losses, pick the largest recoverable category and work it. The unhelpful responses are to add three subjects of tuition, to switch tutors in panic, or to decide the student cannot do the subject. The script tells you which of those the evidence supports, and it is almost never the last one.

sections.heading: Entries, private candidates and the zone trap nobody mentions
paragraphs: If your child is entered through their school, entries are the school's job and your job is to meet the internal cut-off. If your child is sitting as a private candidate, which happens in the northern emirates more than people assume, then entries are entirely yours and there is an administrative detail that can cost a whole paper.

Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and publishes a separate version of the timetable for each. Its own guidance states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. That is as clear a warning as an examination board ever issues, and the fix takes one email to the centre.

The second private-candidate detail is the practical subject question. Cambridge assesses practical skills in some sciences through an alternative-to-practical paper, which a private candidate can sit, while some components require laboratory arrangements a centre has to confirm. Ask the centre which components they can offer for your child's exact syllabus code before paying any entry fee, and ask in writing.

The third is timing. Private-candidate deadlines at independent centres are frequently earlier than school deadlines, because the centre has to aggregate entries. Treat the centre's stated date as the real one, add a fortnight of your own margin, and do the subject and tier decisions before that rather than during it.

sections.heading: What a time-boxed block costs against an open-ended arrangement
paragraphs: Published market rates let you do this arithmetic yourself, which is the point of printing them. A qualified subject tutor working online is quoted at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour across this market, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150. A specialist sits nearer AED 200 to 450, with TutorChase around AED 270. Budget online tuition starts far lower, from about AED 33 to 52 at Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 at EdFlik, and buys supervision rather than syllabus depth.

Now put those numbers into the two structures families actually choose between. An eight-session pre-series block in the qualified band costs roughly the same as five or six weeks of open-ended weekly tuition, and it has an end date, a stated goal and a halfway review. The open-ended arrangement has none of those, which is why it is the one that tends to run for two years and get cancelled in a bad week rather than reviewed in a good one.

In-home tuition sits on top of all of this as a travel charge rather than a quality tier. Market figures put in-home one-to-one at roughly AED 180 to 350 in Bestimate's Dubai rate work and AED 200 to 500 among independent home tutors, with monthly packages seen at about AED 799 for eight online sessions against AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. From Al Salamah the drive is longer than those Dubai figures assume, so the premium is larger and the pool it reaches is smaller.

All of the above are other providers' published figures, cited so you can judge a quote. They are not our price list. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE at any price, and our own conversation begins with a free trial lesson and an argument about how few hours the diagnosis justifies.

sections.heading: Permits, regulators and what a tutor may not do with coursework
paragraphs: Three compliance points belong on any page that asks a family for money, and they are short. First, tutor licensing. Private tutoring in the UAE requires the private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation smart app, website or e-services system, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no schedule of amounts is published, so treat any specific figure as unverified.

Second, school regulation, which follows the campus rather than the home. Private schools in Umm Al Quwain are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, alongside Ajman and Fujairah. A Sharjah campus answers to the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which approves fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Ras Al Khaimah has its own Department of Knowledge with a comparable remit. Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority and Abu Dhabi's Department of Education and Knowledge cover those emirates. IB Gram holds no accreditation from any of them, and a provider claiming otherwise should be asked to produce the permit number.

Third, coursework. IGCSE carries less assessed coursework than the Diploma, but where a component is internally assessed the rule is the same: a tutor teaches, explains, sets practice and gives feedback on the student's own work, and does not produce the work. One site ranking for UAE tutoring queries sells completed assessments outright. The exposure from that falls on the student, not the seller.

The fourth point is not compliance but it belongs here. Do not ask your child's own classroom teacher to tutor privately. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a similar restriction. A different specialist also gives you something more valuable: an independent read on the predicted grade.

process.title: Send the statement of entry
process.description: Board, series, subject codes and paper numbers are all on it, and those four facts change what a tutor should do with the time remaining. If it cannot be found, the front cover of a past paper and a quick question to the subject teacher get you most of the way there.

process.title: One timed paper before any plan
process.description: The first session produces a marked script with every lost mark categorised. That document is what the block is built on, and it very often reorders the subject priority a family arrived with. It is also the baseline you will measure against in week five.

process.title: Agree the number of sessions up front
process.description: Blocks are sized to the diagnosis and the weeks available, and the end date is stated before the first paid lesson. Open-ended arrangements drift; a block with a stated end forces an honest review of whether it worked.

process.title: Halfway review in writing
process.description: At the midpoint the tutor repeats a version of the week-one paper and writes down what moved. If nothing has, that is a reason to change approach or tutor rather than to add sessions, and the note says so plainly.

process.title: Stop at the series
process.description: The block ends with the papers rather than rolling into the next term by default. If the results in August argue for a November resit, that is a new, narrower plan built on the actual paper breakdown rather than a continuation of the old one.

whyPoints.title: The plan starts from the calendar
whyPoints.description: Three weeks out and twenty weeks out are different purchases, and conflating them is how families overpay. A first call here establishes which window you are in and what that window can realistically deliver before anyone discusses hours.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before teaching
whyPoints.description: A strictly marked timed paper costs one session and routinely changes the whole plan. Students are usually wrong about which topic is costing them marks, and so, in the autumn, are reports. The script is not.

whyPoints.title: Time-boxed, not open-ended
whyPoints.description: Blocks have a stated length, a stated goal and a halfway review. The commonest waste in this market is tuition that was useful in March and still being billed in November, and a stated end date is the cheapest protection against it.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the board and the series
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 and Edexcel 4MA1 are both IGCSE Maths and not the same job, and a June candidate and a November resit candidate need different work. Matching on code and series is unglamorous and prevents a wasted first month.

whyPoints.title: Market rates printed, not hidden
whyPoints.description: Three of six ranking competitors publish no price at all and one of them refuses the question inside its own FAQ. The published figures on this page are other providers' numbers, cited so you can judge any quote you receive, including ours.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE series will an Al Salamah student be entered for?
faqs.answer: Cambridge offers a June series and a November series to candidates in the UAE, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May or June and again in November. The February and March series that appears in some search results is offered to India only and is not available to candidates sitting here. June is the main series for most Year 11 cohorts in this region, with November used as the resit route. Your child's statement of entry names the series, the board and the paper numbers, and the board's live official timetable carries the dates.

faqs.question: How early does the school close IGCSE entries?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families expect, and earlier than the board's own deadline. Schools set an internal cut-off so they can aggregate and submit entries, and that internal date is the one that actually binds you. It is also when tier decisions get locked, which matters in Cambridge subjects where a Core entry caps the grade available. If there is a case for moving a child from Core to Extended, it has to be made before that cut-off rather than after the mock results arrive.

faqs.question: Is eight weeks enough time to move a grade in Maths 0580?
faqs.answer: Often yes, because so much of what is lost in this subject is method rather than understanding. Unsimplified exact answers, bearings taken from the wrong line, probability trees never multiplied along the branch and working omitted entirely are all technique failures that a strictly marked paper exposes in one session. Eight weekly sessions with written work between them is roughly twenty hours of focused effort, which is enough for one subject done properly. It is not enough for four, whatever a package says.

faqs.question: What should we do with a disappointing mock result?
faqs.answer: Ask the school for the script, not just the grade. The annotated paper tells you which question types failed, whether the back half was reached and whether long-answer marks were taken, and those habits transfer straight to the real series. The grade itself carries distortions: mocks often use older papers, teacher-estimated boundaries and an incomplete syllabus. Categorise the losses, pick the largest recoverable category and work it. Adding three subjects of tuition in response to one bad mock is the standard expensive mistake.

faqs.question: When should a November resit plan actually start?
faqs.answer: The week the August results arrive, not in October. A resit is a narrower job than first-time preparation because the content is already known and the diagnosis exists in the result breakdown, so the work can be surgical. What kills resits is the gap: families take September to decide, confirm an entry late, and leave six weeks for a plan that needed twelve. Confirm the entry route and the centre's deadline first, then build the paper work backwards from the series.

faqs.question: My son sits as a private candidate. What do I need to check first?
faqs.answer: Three things, in writing. First, the centre's own entry deadline, which is usually earlier than a school's because the centre has to aggregate entries. Second, which components it can offer for your child's exact syllabus code, since some science practical arrangements have to be confirmed. Third, the timetable zone. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that using the correct version for your zone is essential, and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one.

faqs.question: Should we work on content or past papers in the final month?
faqs.answer: Papers, almost always. Technique needs content to operate on, so the content work has to finish roughly eight weeks out to leave a runway. A student still meeting new material three weeks before the papers is learning rather than revising, and the two feel similar while paying very differently. In the final month the highest-yield activities are command-term discipline, time allocation by mark, and full papers under real timing including the sections that normally get skipped.

faqs.question: How much does a pre-series IGCSE block cost in this market?
faqs.answer: Judge it from published figures rather than from a sales call. Qualified online subject tutors are quoted at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour across this market, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and TutorChase around AED 270 in the specialist band. Budget online tuition starts near AED 33 to 65 and buys supervision rather than depth. An eight-session block in the qualified band costs about what five or six weeks of open-ended weekly tuition does, and unlike that arrangement it has an end date.

faqs.question: Can we get an IGCSE tutor who travels to Al Salamah?
faqs.answer: Not from IB Gram. Our in-person visits are an India-only service and we do not send tutors to UAE addresses. Independent home tutors do work in the northern emirates, with market rates quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour once travel is included against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified online subject tutor. From Al Salamah the drive is longer than those Dubai-derived figures assume, so you pay more for travel and choose from a smaller specialist pool. A free trial lesson lets you test the online format against your own child.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with my child need a licence in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it does not cost anything. The private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation smart app, website or e-services, with a stated two-working-day completion time. Registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18 are all eligible to apply. Anyone offering private lessons without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: Which regulator inspects a school my Umm Al Quwain child attends in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: The Sharjah Private Education Authority, because regulation follows the campus and not your home address. SPEA approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods in that emirate, which is a wider remit than inspection alone. Private schools in Umm Al Quwain itself are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, alongside Ajman and Fujairah. If the campus is in Ras Al Khaimah, that emirate's Department of Knowledge takes the same role, so inspection reports and fee approvals all sit with the school.

faqs.question: Can a tutor finish my daughter's internally assessed coursework for her?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider agreeing to it is selling your daughter a risk rather than a service. A tutor teaches, explains, sets practice, marks and gives feedback on work the student has produced. Supplying text or completing an assessed component is malpractice, and the consequence lands on the candidate rather than on the tutor. At least one site ranking for UAE tutoring queries sells completed assessments outright, which is worth knowing when you are comparing options on price alone.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tuition in Year 10 if nothing is going wrong yet?
faqs.answer: It is the best value available in the qualification, and almost nobody buys it. Roughly two-thirds of the examined content is delivered in Year 10 and then left alone until revision, which is why Year 11 students appear to have forgotten everything. An hour a week that tracks the school's current topics and keeps revisiting the autumn ones prevents the backlog that later costs a twenty-session rescue. Families who start here reliably buy fewer total hours than families who start in the spring of Year 11.

faqs.question: How many subjects should we actually pay for at once?
faqs.answer: One, usually, and two at most in an exam year. The arithmetic is simple: eight weekly sessions plus the written work between them is roughly twenty to twenty-five hours of real effort, which moves one subject properly or makes partial progress in two. Spread across four, it produces a tired student and four unchanged grades. Use the marked mock scripts to choose, because the subject a family is most anxious about is frequently not the subject where the most marks are recoverable.
